ops.notes:
# FamilySearch Wiki: Irish church records

Church records are among the most important sources for Irish genealogy research. The two main denominations that kept parish registers in Ireland were the Roman Catholic Church and the Church of Ireland (Anglican). Roman Catholic registers generally begin in the early 1800s, while Church of Ireland registers often start earlier, in the 1700s. Many original registers were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office fire, but microfilmed copies and transcriptions survive. FamilySearch has digitized and indexed a large collection of Irish Catholic and Church of Ireland parish registers, which are freely searchable at FamilySearch.org. To find Irish church records on FamilySearch, go to FamilySearch.org and click Search, then Records. Enter your ancestor's name and select Ireland as the country. Filter results by record type to narrow to church records including baptisms, marriages, and burials. The National Library of Ireland also holds a large collection of Catholic parish registers on microfilm, many of which have been digitized and are available online. The Representative Church Body Library in Dublin holds Church of Ireland registers not destroyed in 1922.

Irish church records typically contain baptism (christening) records listing the child's name, baptism date, parents' names, and sometimes the townland or parish of residence. Marriage records list the names of the bride and groom, the date and place of marriage, and witnesses. Burial records list the name of the deceased and the burial date. Earlier records may contain less detail. Some registers also include sponsor names for baptisms, which can help identify other family members.

## Sources

- [Ireland Church Records — Overview of Irish Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records#Overview_of_Irish_Church_Records)
- [Ireland Church Records — Finding Church Records on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records#Finding_Church_Records_on_FamilySearch)
- [Ireland Church Records — What Church Records Contain](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records#What_Church_Records_Contain)

ops.notes:
# FamilySearch Wiki: Italian birth records

Civil registration (Stato Civile) of births, marriages, and deaths began in most of Italy in 1809 under Napoleonic rule, lapsed in many regions after 1815, and resumed nationwide in 1866 following unification. Civil birth records (atti di nascita) are the single most useful source for Italian genealogy after 1866. They record the child's name, the date and place of birth, and the names, ages, occupations, and residence of both parents.

Before civil registration, and as a parallel source afterward, Catholic parish registers (registri parrocchiali) recorded baptisms. A baptismal record (atto di battesimo) usually gives the baptism date, the child's name, the parents' names, and the godparents. Parish registers in many Italian dioceses begin in the late 1500s following the Council of Trent.

Many Italian civil registration records have been digitized and are listed in the FamilySearch Catalog, searchable by the comune (town) where the event occurred. Records less than 100 years old are generally restricted by Italian privacy law and must be requested directly from the local Ufficio dello Stato Civile.

## Sources

# FamilySearch Wiki: Italian birth records

Civil registration (Stato Civile) of births, marriages, and deaths began in most of Italy in 1809 under Napoleonic rule, lapsed in many regions after 1815, and resumed nationwide in 1866 following unification. Civil birth records (atti di nascita) are the single most useful source for Italian genealogy after 1866. They record the child's name, the date and place of birth, and the names, ages, occupations, and residence of both parents.

Before civil registration, and as a parallel source afterward, Catholic parish registers (registri parrocchiali) recorded baptisms. A baptismal record (atto di battesimo) usually gives the baptism date, the child's name, the parents' names, and the godparents. Parish registers in many Italian dioceses begin in the late 1500s following the Council of Trent.

Many Italian civil registration records have been digitized and are listed in the FamilySearch Catalog, searchable by the comune (town) where the event occurred. Records less than 100 years old are generally restricted by Italian privacy law and must be requested directly from the local Ufficio dello Stato Civile.

# FamilySearch Wiki: German church records

Church records (Kirchenbücher) are the most important source for German genealogy before civil registration. Many German church records have been microfilmed or digitized and are listed in the FamilySearch Catalog under the parish or town name. Others remain only at the parish, the regional church archive (Landeskirchliches Archiv or Kirchenbuchamt), or on subscription sites such as Archion (Protestant) and Matricula (Catholic).

# FamilySearch Wiki: immigration records

Immigration records document the arrival of individuals into a country and are a key source for tracing ancestors who moved from one country to another. For the United States, passenger arrival records (also called ship manifests or passenger lists) are the primary immigration records. These records were created at the port of arrival and typically list the passenger's name, age, occupation, country of origin, and destination. FamilySearch has a large free collection of U.S. passenger arrival records searchable by name at FamilySearch.org. To find immigration records on FamilySearch, go to FamilySearch.org, click Search, then Records, and enter your ancestor's name. You can filter by record type and country of origin to narrow results. Naturalization records are also useful, as they document the process by which an immigrant became a citizen and may include the immigrant's country of birth, arrival date, and port of entry. Naturalization records were kept at the local court level and FamilySearch has indexed many of them.

Marriage records in the United States were typically kept by county clerks, churches, or state vital records offices depending on the time period and location. # FamilySearch Wiki: Civil War military service records

Civil War military records are held primarily at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. For Union soldiers, Compiled Military Service Records (CMSRs) document a soldier's service and are available through Fold3 (a subscription site) and in some cases through FamilySearch. Pension files, which may include personal statements, medical records, and family information, are also held at the National Archives and are rich genealogical sources. FamilySearch has indexed some Civil War pension indexes that can help you identify whether a pension file exists. For Confederate soldiers, records are more scattered because many Confederate records were destroyed or never created. State archives for the former Confederate states hold the most complete collections. Some Confederate pension records are available at state archives. FamilySearch has digitized and indexed several Confederate military collections. Searching by state is often more productive than a nationwide search for Confederate ancestors.

## Sources

- [United States Civil War Records — Military Service Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Civil_War_Records#Military_Service_Records)
- [United States Civil War Records — Confederate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Civil_War_Records#Confederate_Records)

ops.notes:
# FamilySearch Wiki: probate or will records for a deceased ancestor

Probate records are created when a deceased person's estate is settled through a court process. They include wills, inventories of property, letters of administration, and final settlements. Probate records can identify family members (especially heirs), provide an economic snapshot, and confirm dates and places. In the United States, probate is handled at the county level; records are held by county probate courts or surrogate courts. FamilySearch has indexed and digitized probate records from many counties across the country. To find probate records on FamilySearch, search the FamilySearch Catalog by state and county under the 'Probate records' category. Many collections are browse-only images. When a will is found, read it carefully — testators often name children, grandchildren, and in-laws by name. Intestate records (for those who died without a will) list heirs and their relationships to the deceased, which can be equally valuable for establishing family connections.

## Sources

- [United States Probate Records — What Are Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Probate_Records#What_Are_Probate_Records)
- [United States Probate Records — Finding Probate Records on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Probate_Records#Finding_Probate_Records_on_FamilySearch)
